Frank is awesome, but I believe the data he is being provided is incredibly misleading in this situation.

You can’t simply exclude quarterback sneaks from the under center population and then conclude that shotgun is better. That removes a central part of what makes being under center valuable.

I don’t buy the idea that only three or four teams can sneak effectively. Over the last eight seasons, 26 NFL franchises converted at least 81% of their QB sneaks on 3rd/4th & 1.

In my view, forcing defenses to account for the sneak is a major advantage in short yardage. If they don’t defend it, take it. If they sell out to stop it, you’ve created opportunities to attack elsewhere.

And being under center doesn’t mean you have to sneak.

When defenses had defenders on the line occupying both A gaps and both B gaps, passes from under center on 4th & 1 converted 74.4% of the time and averaged +1.28 EPA/play.

Against those same interior looks, pin and pull concepts and jet sweeps both converted over 82% of the time with one yard to go. These concepts illustrate the complementary options available.

The defense’s commitment to stopping one yard inside can create an opportunity for a much bigger play outside.

Moving into shotgun takes the conventional sneak off the table. The broader comparison matters: on 4th & 1, runs and passes from under center combined converted 70.9%, versus 65.3% from shotgun.

Perhaps most importantly, not all shotgun runs present the same threats.

Shotgun runs with a QB run, read option or RPO component:
73.2% conversion, +0.68 EPA/play.

Shotgun runs without those components:
64.5% conversion, +0.08 EPA/play.

That second group was also below runs from under center excluding sneaks: 66.2% conversion and +0.22 EPA/play.

The Jets’ failed play was a simple handoff with no QB run, read option or RPO component. Applying the overall shotgun run average to that play glosses over a meaningful distinction.

My preferred approach remains: line up under cent

Have gotten this question a couple times before: In a vacuum if you believe your chance of converting a 2 point attempt is statistically significant vs the other team’s, then it’s probably worth it to do it

However, it’s almost always not going to be statistically significant. When you go for 2 up 7 you end up giving the other team a big information advantage that they wouldn’t otherwise get if they were down 8

If you go up 9, then the other team knows they have to be hyper aggressive to score, get the ball back and then try to score again

If you miss the 2 point and are up 7 then the other team knows they can operate as if they just need a TD 

But if you go up 8 by kicking the XP, the other team could go down and score but not know whether they’ll need another possession until sometimes when it’s too late

KC Concepcion

KC’s NFL career is off to a fine albeit not fantastic start, as he’s posted a just okay 0.22 TPRR and 1.58 YPRR, while sitting 1 target shy of the team lead in targets. That’s certainly influenced by underwhelming QB play (although Watson has not been as bad as expected), but I think we see Concepcion show why he was a 1st round pick here in Week 3.

For starters, the Panthers have been notably weaker against the slot since 2025. With Jaycee Horn and Michael Jackson on the outside, opposing teams have generally looked to win with their slot/inline players. Carolina was 22nd in YPG allowed to the slot last year, while 3rd best in wide YPG allowed. For the likely best target-earning player in this pass-catching group who has the 9th highest slot rate in the NFL (71.1%), this could be a good chance for him to earn 6+ targets in this one.

The Panthers also run a ton of single-high safety looks, doing so at the 3rd highest rate in 2026 at nearly 70% of the time per @FantasyPtsData. It’s obviously a rather small sample, but KC has been cooking vs. single-high. He jumps up to 2.48 YPRR (+56.9%) and 0.33 TPRR (+50%) against these looks, massive boosts over his baseline.

I think KC is quite undervalued at his 32.5 receiving-yard line, especially relative to Denzel Boston who’s sitting just shy of 50 (49.5 o/u).
